info.title: Weft Platform API
info.description: Control-plane and Repos API for Weft: git-shaped storage served from object storage. Git smart-HTTP endpoints (clone/fetch/push at /{org}/{repo}.git) speak the standard git wire protocol and are not described here. Errors return JSON {"error": "…"} with the matching status. Optimistic-concurrency conflicts return 409 with the current tip.

bearer.description: Token of the form weft_<id>_<secret>. Scopes: org:admin, org:read, repo:read, repo:write. Repo-bound tokens are restricted to one repo.

session.name: stratum_session
session.description: Browser session from POST /v1/auth/login. An alternative to a bearer token for the dashboard; a bearer token wins when both are presented. Routes under /v1/auth use this scheme.

self_hosted_repos.description: Repository names, sorted. Only consulted under `selected`, but returned always so a dashboard switching back still has the list somebody chose.

allow_public.description: Whether public repositories may reach the machines in this group. False by default, and that default is the security property rather than a preference: a public repository can be forked, and a fork's change carries its own `run:` lines.

runners.description: How many live machines are in it.

labels.description: What this machine will match. The server always adds `self-hosted`, the OS and the architecture to whatever custom labels it offered.

ephemeral.description: Registered to run one job and then de-register.

state.description: Derived, never stored: `busy` if a running job points at it, else `online` if it called within the last 60 seconds, else `offline`. There is no status column for a crashed process to leave lying.

job.description: What it is running right now, or null.

job_id.description: The workflow job's row id — what a link into the run needs.

repo.description: The repository's name — not its id. A run is addressed by `owner/repo`, so this is what a link to the build needs.

stored_bytes.description: What this repository holds in the object store, in bytes, as of the last push or storage sweep. For a private repository it is what the organization's storage meter counts, averaged over the billing period; a public repository's storage is never counted. Precision is one push: the push gate checks the bytes it is about to write against the pool and the spend limit before it writes.

origin_url.description: Origin identity for a mirror — a fetchable URL for the generic provider, or "owner/name" for the GitHub App provider. Null for native repos.

clone_url.description: HTTPS git remote for this repo.

ssh_clone_url.description: SSH git remote (ssh://git@host:port/org/repo.git), or null when the deployment has no SSH front door configured.

origin_provider.description: Origin integration backing a mirror; null for native repos.

origin_installation.description: GitHub App installation id used to mint fetch credentials for this mirror; null unless origin_provider is "github".

homepage.description: The project's own address on the web, shown in the repository's About panel. Always an absolute http:// or https:// URL, or null — a scheme-less "example.com" is refused rather than repaired, because prepending a scheme is wrong in exactly the case that matters: a relative URL resolving against this host, wearing the project's name. Empty and whitespace-only are stored as null, so "no homepage" has one encoding rather than two.

fork_count.description: Public repositories forked directly from this one. The count a caller may see, not a stored total — a fork can be made private after the fact, so publishing the stored number would reveal how many private forks exist.

watcher_count.description: People subscribed to everything that happens here. Counts only the "all" watch level: the default subscription is stored as no row at all, so counting the table would rise when somebody chose to be left alone. Public, and on this view rather than on .../watch — that endpoint is the caller's own setting and refuses a stranger, so a masthead reading it would have no number to draw until sign-in and then grow one.

fork_state.description: Fork preparation state; absent on a repository that is not a fork. A fork's row exists immediately and its storage pointers a moment later, which is why forking answers 202.

org.description: The namespace this repository is in, by name. The row carries org_id, which is no use to a client: after forking into 'wherever I belong', the answer to 'where did it go' is a name.

commits.description: How many commits are reachable from the default branch's tip — every parent of every commit, as GitHub counts — as of the last time the compaction job that follows every write counted them. Null until it has. Stored rather than computed on the request: a repository page must not walk history to print a number.

commits_tip.description: The commit `commits` was counted from. A client that knows the current tip compares the two and shows the number only while they agree, rather than printing a count that is a push behind as though it were current.

commits_exact.description: False when the walk stopped at STRATUM_COMMIT_COUNT_CAP (default 100000) with history still to go; the true number is then at least `commits`. True when there is no count yet, so a client has one flag to read.

fork_parent.description: owner/name of what this was forked from, when the viewer may see it. Null covers three different facts on purpose: not a fork, upstream deleted and this promoted, or an upstream this viewer may not see — which is why it cannot be derived client-side from an id.

viewer_admin.description: Whether the caller may administer this repository — visibility, default branch, branch protections, access. Answered by the server because the two authorities differ: patch and the protections routes accept a per-repo admin grant, while the access listing requires org-wide admin, so a client inferring one from the other hides the settings surface from somebody entitled to it. false for an anonymous reader.

viewer_member.description: Whether the caller holds a role on this repository — an organization membership or a per-repo grant — as opposed to reading it because it is public. The distinction only exists on a public repository and is what the Insights tab turns on: a repository's traffic belongs to the people who own it. Weaker than `viewer_write`: the `viewer` role is a member who may not push. false for an anonymous reader and for a signed-in stranger alike.

viewer_write.description: Whether the caller may push here, and so whether they may open a change whose commits are already in this repository. Distinct from viewer_admin: a member writes without administering, and an outside contributor reads without either. Answered by the server because it is the scope POST /changes actually checks before refusing a change that names no source — a client guessing it either hides the form from somebody who may use it, or offers one to a stranger and refuses them after they have filled it in. false for an anonymous reader.

write_blocked.description: Why nobody may write to this repository right now — the sentence a push is refused with, beginning `quota:` — or null when writes are allowed. About the repository and not the caller, so a page can say read-only to a reader too, and folded into viewer_write, which is false whenever this is set. The case is a private repository on an organization whose subscription has ended, or one with no card on file yet: it used to look exactly like any other repository until git push answered 402 with a sentence nobody had seen.

push.description: For a mirror: whether a push to it is forwarded to its origin, and if not, why. null for a native repository. `forwarding` is the answer; `blocked` is the sentence a push would be refused with; `needs_permission` with `approve_url` is an installation that predates `Contents: write`.

expected_parent.description: Optimistic concurrency: the branch must currently point here (null = branch must not exist; omitted = commit on the current tip).

context.description: Free-form audit blob recorded immutably with the commit.

org.description: Namespace name — a repo name alone is ambiguous across namespaces.

post.summary: actions/cache asks whether an archive is saved (cache service v2)
post.description: Not a route a person calls. The credential is the job's **cache token** (`github:cache`), handed to a runner with its registration and carried by the cache proxy in the container; it names the job, the job names the repository, and the repository is the scope. From anywhere else — a GitHub-hosted runner, via `weftsh/cache` — the credential is a **`repo:cache` token** minted like any other, and the repository is named in the `X-Weft-Repository` header as `owner/name`; the scope is the same (org, GitHub full name), so a save from either kind of runner is a hit for the other. Refusals are ordered 401 (no or unknown token), 403 (a token of another kind, or a repo:cache token restricted to one Weft repository), 400 (a repo:cache token with no usable header), 410 (the job is over). The body is `{key, version, restore_keys?}` as the client sends it (snake_case); the answer is `{ok, signed_download_url, matched_key}` — the exact key if a ready entry has it, else the newest under a restore-key prefix, else `ok: false`, which the client reads as a miss.

200.description: { ok, signed_download_url, matched_key }

400.description: Malformed body

401.description: No token, or one that does not authenticate

403.description: A token not minted for the cache

410.description: The job this token was minted for is over

post.description: Not a route a person calls. The credential is the job's **cache token** (`github:cache`), handed to a runner with its registration and carried by the cache proxy in the container; it names the job, the job names the repository, and the repository is the scope. From anywhere else — a GitHub-hosted runner, via `weftsh/cache` — the credential is a **`repo:cache` token** minted like any other, and the repository is named in the `X-Weft-Repository` header as `owner/name`; the scope is the same (org, GitHub full name), so a save from either kind of runner is a hit for the other. Refusals are ordered 401 (no or unknown token), 403 (a token of another kind, or a repo:cache token restricted to one Weft repository), 400 (a repo:cache token with no usable header), 410 (the job is over). `{key, version}` reserves the entry for this repository and answers `{ok, signed_upload_url}`; a key already saved or being saved answers `ok: false`, which the client reads as "already exists" and skips its save.

200.description: { ok, signed_upload_url }

400.description: Malformed body

401.description: No token

403.description: A token not minted for the cache

post.summary: actions/cache finishes a save
post.description: Not a route a person calls. The credential is the job's **cache token** (`github:cache`), handed to a runner with its registration and carried by the cache proxy in the container; it names the job, the job names the repository, and the repository is the scope. From anywhere else — a GitHub-hosted runner, via `weftsh/cache` — the credential is a **`repo:cache` token** minted like any other, and the repository is named in the `X-Weft-Repository` header as `owner/name`; the scope is the same (org, GitHub full name), so a save from either kind of runner is a hit for the other. Refusals are ordered 401 (no or unknown token), 403 (a token of another kind, or a repo:cache token restricted to one Weft repository), 400 (a repo:cache token with no usable header), 410 (the job is over). `{key, version, size_bytes}` closes the reservation: the size must equal what the blob route received, and the entry becomes restorable.

200.description: { ok, entry_id }

400.description: Nothing uploaded, or the size disagrees with what arrived

404.description: No upload in progress under that key and version

409.description: Already finalized

401.description: No token

403.description: A token not minted for the cache

put.summary: The signed upload URL: the archive's bytes
put.description: Not a route a person calls. The credential is the job's **cache token** (`github:cache`), handed to a runner with its registration and carried by the cache proxy in the container; it names the job, the job names the repository, and the repository is the scope. From anywhere else — a GitHub-hosted runner, via `weftsh/cache` — the credential is a **`repo:cache` token** minted like any other, and the repository is named in the `X-Weft-Repository` header as `owner/name`; the scope is the same (org, GitHub full name), so a save from either kind of runner is a hit for the other. Refusals are ordered 401 (no or unknown token), 403 (a token of another kind, or a repo:cache token restricted to one Weft repository), 400 (a repo:cache token with no usable header), 410 (the job is over). What the client's Azure block-blob upload sends: one PUT for an archive up to 128 MiB, or blocks (`?comp=block&blockid=…`) followed by a block list (`?comp=blocklist`, Azure's XML) giving the archive's order. Only while the entry is reserving.

201.description: Stored

400.description: An empty body, a block list naming a block that never arrived, or an unsupported `comp`

404.description: No such entry for this repository

409.description: The entry is already finalized

401.description: No token

403.description: A token not minted for the cache

get.description: Not a route a person calls. The credential is the job's **cache token** (`github:cache`), handed to a runner with its registration and carried by the cache proxy in the container; it names the job, the job names the repository, and the repository is the scope. From anywhere else — a GitHub-hosted runner, via `weftsh/cache` — the credential is a **`repo:cache` token** minted like any other, and the repository is named in the `X-Weft-Repository` header as `owner/name`; the scope is the same (org, GitHub full name), so a save from either kind of runner is a hit for the other. Refusals are ordered 401 (no or unknown token), 403 (a token of another kind, or a repo:cache token restricted to one Weft repository), 400 (a repo:cache token with no usable header), 410 (the job is over). Streams the archive's blocks in order; honours `Range` (206 with `Content-Range`), because the client downloads a large archive in concurrent ranged GETs.

200.description: The archive

404.description: No such ready entry for this repository

401.description: No token

403.description: A token not minted for the cache

get.summary: What kinds of runner this organisation allows (org:read)
get.description: Two independent switches, because they answer opposite questions. `hosted` is "may our work run on Weft's machines"; `self_hosted` is "may our work run on machines we registered". An organisation that only trusts its own hardware turns the first off; one that does not want a stranger's change near its build box turns the second off.

200.description: The policy as it stands

patch.description: Any subset of the three keys; an absent key is left alone. `self_hosted_repos` is a list of repository names and is replaced wholesale — `[]` clears it. Audited as `runner_policy.updated`. A refusal here is a refusal at trigger time rather than a job queued forever: a `runs-on: ubuntu-latest` file under `hosted: disabled` becomes a failed run reading "hosted runners are disabled for this organisation; use runs-on: [self-hosted, …]".

self_hosted_repos.description: Repository names in this organisation. A name that is not there is a 422 rather than a silent drop: a group that quietly admits four of the five somebody listed is a build that does not run and a settings page that says it should.

200.description: The policy as it now stands

404.description: No such organisation, or the caller is not an admin of it

422.description: A value outside the enumeration, or a repository name that is not there

get.summary: Runner groups in this organisation (org:read)
get.description: A group is the unit a repository is admitted by, and every machine is in exactly one. Every organisation has a `default` group, created lazily the first time anything needs one — so this never answers an empty list.

200.description: { groups: […] }

post.summary: Create a runner group (org:admin)
post.description: `repo_access` defaults to `all` and `allow_public` to false. Audited as `runner_group.created`.

repos.description: Repository names in this organisation. A name that is not there is a 422 rather than a silent drop: a group that quietly admits four of the five somebody listed is a build that does not run and a settings page that says it should.

201.description: Created

404.description: No such organisation, or the caller is not an admin of it

409.description: A group of that name already exists

422.description: An invalid name or `repo_access`, or a repository name that is not there

patch.description: Any subset; an absent key is left alone, and `repos` is replaced wholesale. The default group's name is fixed (422): it is the name printed in every registration command ever handed out, and renaming it would silently point those at nothing. Audited as `runner_group.updated`.

repos.description: Repository names in this organisation. A name that is not there is a 422 rather than a silent drop: a group that quietly admits four of the five somebody listed is a build that does not run and a settings page that says it should.

200.description: The group as it now stands

404.description: No such group in this organisation

409.description: Another group already has that name

422.description: An invalid value, or an attempt to rename the default group

delete.summary: Delete a runner group (org:admin)
delete.description: Its machines move to the default group rather than being removed: an operator tidying their groups has not asked to take thirty machines offline, and a runner whose group vanished would authenticate and then never be routed anything — the least debuggable failure this feature has. Any outstanding registration token for the group goes with it. The default group cannot be deleted. Audited as `runner_group.deleted`.

204.description: Deleted; its machines are now in the default group

404.description: No such group in this organisation

get.summary: The machines this organisation has registered (org:read)
get.description: Live machines only. A removed one is tombstoned rather than deleted — a job row names the machine that ran it, and a reader looking at last week's build should still be told which — but it is gone from here.

200.description: { runners: […] }

post.summary: Mint a single-use registration token (org:admin)
post.description: One hour, one machine. Hashed at rest like every other bearer secret here, because it travels through a shell history and a terminal scrollback on its way to the machine. `command` is the whole `weft-runner register` line spelled out — the alternative is a reader assembling it from three fields and getting `--url` wrong, which fails at registration with a network error that says nothing about which part was wrong. Audited as `runner.registration_token.created`.

group.description: The group the machine will join.

201.description: The only time the token exists

404.description: No such organisation, or the caller is not an admin of it

delete.summary: Remove a machine (org:admin)
delete.description: Its credential is dead from the next call it makes — which is the whole revocation mechanism, since nothing is listening on the operator's network to be told. A job running on it is failed, with the error "runner removed while the job was running", and deliberately not handed to the next machine in the group: an operator who removes a runner has decided the machine should stop, and a silent re-run somewhere else is the opposite of what they asked for. Audited as `runner.removed`.

404.description: No such machine in this organisation

post.summary: Exchange a registration token for the machine's own credential
post.description: Not a route a person calls, and not a session or an API token: the bearer here is the one-hour `weftg_…` secret from the registration-token route, and it names the organisation and the group, so the machine never has to assert either. Every way the token can be wrong — malformed, unknown, already spent, expired — is the same 401, so it cannot be used to learn which organisations exist. Registering under a name that is already live replaces that machine, tombstoning the old row in the same transaction: that is how a credential is rotated, and how a reimaged machine comes back without somebody having to remove it by hand first. Audited as `runner.registered`.

name.description: Letters, digits, dot, dash, underscore; at most 64. Defaults to the hostname on the runner side.

labels.description: Custom labels only. `self-hosted`, the OS and the architecture are added by the server, so a job's `runs-on` can rely on them being there.

ephemeral.description: Run one job, then de-register. The autoscaling shape.

201.description: The only time the credential exists

credential.description: `weftr_…`. Hashed at rest and never recoverable; re-register to get another.

401.description: The registration token is unknown, already used or expired

422.description: A name, label, OS or architecture outside what is allowed

post.summary: Ask for work, and wait a while for some
post.description: The bearer is the machine's own `weftr_…` credential. A long poll: the server holds the request open for `STRATUM_RUNNER_CLAIM_WAIT_MS` (20 s by default), re-running its claim every 500 ms, and answers 204 if nothing came. That is the whole scaling story — asking every second is one query per machine per second forever, almost all of it answering "nothing"; asking every thirty is half a minute of latency on every build. Set the client's HTTP timeout longer than the server's wait, so a 204 arrives as a 204 rather than as a client-side timeout. Every call touches `last_seen_at`, which is what the runner list's `online` reading is made of. A job is routed to this machine only if its `runs-on` labels are a subset of the machine's, the machine's group admits the repository (and `allow_public` if it is public), and the organisation's policy admits self-hosted runners for it — three different people's decisions, all re-read here and not only at trigger time, because a job can sit in the queue across a settings change. On 200 the machine then uses exactly the five per-job calls a hosted runner uses, with the `token` from here.

200.description: A job was assigned

token.description: The per-job, per-attempt credential for the five runner calls: `repo:read` on one repository, revoked the moment the verdict lands.

runner_url.description: The base URL to report on — the address this machine already reached, not the public one. They are the same behind a CDN and differ on a private network.

204.description: Nothing to run after the wait. Ask again.

401.description: This credential is unknown, or the machine has been removed. The runner prints that it has been removed and exits: there is no way back without registering.

409.description: { error: "busy" } — this machine already holds a running job. A runner runs one job at a time, and a second would be work nobody ever reports on.

get.summary: A person's public profile
get.description: Display name, bio, location, company, pronouns, account kind (human or agent), links, and how many public repositories their namespace holds. Open to anonymous callers — this is the page a logged-out visitor lands on. It never carries an email address and never a private repository, and `public_repos` counts public repositories for every caller alike, so it cannot be watched to learn that a private one was created. A disabled account has no profile and answers 404; its namespace stays claimed so nobody can move in behind them.

200.description: { handle, name, display_name, bio, location, company, pronouns, kind, contrib_private_optin, profile_repo, created_at, links: [{ label, url }], public_repos }

404.description: No such handle, or the account is disabled

patch.description: Every field is optional: an absent key leaves it alone, an explicit null clears it. `links` replaces the whole list (at most 5) and every url must be http or https — a profile link is rendered as an anchor on a page other people load, so `javascript:` and `data:` are refused. Nobody may patch anybody else's profile.

200.description: The profile as it now reads

400.description: A field is over its cap, holds a control character, or a link is not http(s)

401.description: Not signed in

403.description: This is somebody else's account

404.description: No such handle

get.summary: Somebody's contribution graph
get.description:
One square per day, derived from the commits themselves rather than from activity on this platform — which is what makes a migrated history show up the moment it mirrors over. A commit counts only on one of two grounds: **email-verified**, the author address is a *proved* address on the account, or **pushed-by**, the credential that pushed it was that person's. An address nobody has proved counts for nothing, because anybody can write any string into `git config user.email`. Commit signatures are out of scope. A commit carrying a `Co-Authored-By` trailer is agent-assisted and counts for nobody.

Private work appears only as a **number**, and only when its owner has opted in: `count` includes it, `repos` never names it, and there is no field holding it separately. `private_included` is false both for somebody opted out and for somebody with no private work — deliberately the same answer, since telling those apart would publish the existence of private work.

Anonymous, and the same for every reader: a public page that says different things to different people is one nobody can quote. `from`/`to` are `YYYY-MM-DD` and default to the year ending today; at most 3653 days.

200.description: { from, to, total, private_included, days: [{ day, date, count, repos: [{ org, name, count }] }] } — only days with something on them

400.description: A date that is not YYYY-MM-DD, a range that ends before it starts, or one longer than 3653 days

404.description: No such handle

get.summary: Follower and following counts, and your own edge
get.description: Anonymous readers are welcome and see `you_follow: false`. The counts are counts of a public act.

200.description: { followers, following, you_follow }

404.description: No such handle

put.summary: Follow this person
put.description: Following twice is following once. Following yourself is refused in a sentence rather than reaching the table's CHECK, which would surface as a 500.

200.description: The counts as they now read

400.description: You cannot follow yourself

401.description: Following is a person's act — not signed in, or a service token

404.description: No such handle

delete.summary: Unfollow this person
delete.description: Unfollowing somebody you never followed is a request for the state you are already in, not an error.

200.description: The counts as they now read

401.description: Following is a person's act — not signed in, or a service token

404.description: No such handle

get.summary: Who follows this person
get.description: Newest first, at most 100. Suspended accounts are absent — their public page is down, so naming them would link to a 404.

200.description: { people: [{ handle, display_name }] }

404.description: No such handle

get.summary: Who this person follows
get.description: Newest first, at most 100. Suspended accounts are absent.

200.description: { people: [{ handle, display_name }] }

404.description: No such handle

get.summary: The repositories pinned to a profile
get.description: Filtered to what the caller may see. A pinned repository that has since been made private, or deleted, is absent: `public` is a flag its owner can flip after pinning, so a write-time refusal alone could never cover it.

200.description: { pins: [{ kind, org, name, description, public }] }

404.description: No such handle

put.summary: Replace your pin list (at most 6)
put.description: Body: { pins: [{ org, repo, kind? }] }; only `repo` may be pinned. A private repository can never be pinned. Repositories are resolved through the caller's own visibility first, so naming one they cannot see answers “no such repository” — the same thing a name that does not exist answers — rather than turning the pin form into an existence oracle for every private repository on the platform.

200.description: The pin list as it now reads

400.description: Over the cap, a duplicate, a private repository, an unknown repository, or a kind other than repo

401.description: Not signed in

403.description: This is somebody else's account

404.description: No such handle

get.summary: The addresses on your own account, proved or not
get.description: Never public, and never readable by another account. This is the authorship-linkage surface — the set that decides which commits in the world count as this person's work — so publishing it would hand an impersonator the exact string to put in `git config user.email`, and a spammer a mailbox.

200.description: { emails: [{ address, verified_at, private, primary, created_at }] }

401.description: Not signed in

403.description: This is somebody else's account

404.description: No such handle

post.summary: Claim an address and mail it a confirmation link
post.description: Body: { email }. The claim is worth nothing on its own: the row lands unproved, and only a verified address may ever carry authorship. The link goes to the mailbox and never into the response — a claim confirmed over the API would prove nothing. It is bound both to the address and to this account, so it cannot be spent against a different mailbox or from a different session. At most 10 addresses per account.

400.description: Not an address, or the account is at its address limit

401.description: Not signed in

403.description: This is somebody else's account

409.description: Already yours, or already in use. Which account holds it is never disclosed.

post.summary: Spend a confirmation link and mark that one address proved
post.description: Body: { token }. Every wrong shape — malformed, unknown, expired, already spent, or issued to another account — answers the same 404, so a link cannot be used to ask which addresses are registered here.

200.description: { address, verified: true }

401.description: Not signed in

403.description: This is somebody else's account

404.description: This confirmation link is not valid any more

delete.summary: Drop an address from your account
delete.description: The address you sign in with is refused — an account with no reachable address is one nobody can recover — and so is an address that is not yours, with the same answer.

401.description: Not signed in

403.description: This is somebody else's account

404.description: No such address on this account, or it is the address you sign in with

get.summary: An organization's public face
get.description: Display name, description, location, website, contact address, and its public repository count. Open to anonymous callers. An org that has never been edited reads exactly like one whose fields were cleared — there is no second “no profile yet” state for a page to handle.

200.description: { org, display_name, description, location, website, contact_email, public_repos }

404.description: No such org

patch.description: Optional fields; an explicit null clears one. `website` must be http or https and `contact_email` must be an address, for the same reason the personal profile holds them to it: both are rendered on a page anybody loads.

200.description: The profile as it now reads

400.description: A field is over its cap, the website is not http(s), or the contact address is not an address

401.description: No credential

403.description: Needs org:admin

404.description: No such org, or the caller is not a member

post.summary: Sign in with email and password; sets an HttpOnly session cookie. Every failure — unknown address, wrong password, disabled account — answers 401 identically.

200.description: { id, email, name, created_at, orgs: [{ id, name, role }] }

401.description: invalid email or password

post.summary: End this session and clear the cookie. Answers 204 even without a valid session — a stale cookie still has to go.

get.summary: The signed-in person and the orgs they can reach (session cookie)

Answers a redirect into the dashboard either way, carrying `github=ok|new|denied|expired|noemail|emailtaken|disabled|unavailable|error`; `ok` and `new` also set the session cookie, and `new` is the only one with onboarding left to do.

The changeset's composed CI (`checks` on `GET …/changesets/{changeset}`) is folded into `gate` with the same precedence, blocked over waiting over ready: any composed check failing, cancelled or skipped blocks and `explanation` names it (`composed check {name} in {repo} is {state}`); otherwise any composed check queued or running waits and is listed in `waiting_on` as `{repo}: {name}` (a member's own check is `repo/change: check`); a changeset with no composed checks, or none that can be composed, leaves the gate to its members

404.description: No such changeset, or a member the caller may not read

get.summary: The changeset as one checkout: every member at its proposed head, and the composed clone URL that checks them all out there. repo:read on every member; otherwise 404.

200.description: { key, title, state, composition, tip, clone_url, ssh_clone_url, members: [{ repo, change, title, path, commit, fetch_ref, clone_url, ssh_clone_url }], note } — `clone_url` (and `ssh_clone_url`, null when the server has no SSH front door) is a read-only git repository served for this changeset: one commit on branch `workspace` whose tree holds one submodule per member, at `path` (the repository's name), pinned to `commit`, with `.gitmodules` naming each member by a relative URL so `git clone --recurse-submodules <clone_url>` checks every member out at its proposed head over the same transport and credential. `tip` is that commit; `composition` is the same hash the changeset's composed CI runs are named by, and both move together whenever a member gains a patchset or the membership changes. `fetch_ref` is where each member's commit can be fetched from its own repository even when no branch points at it. Pushing to `clone_url` is refused in-band. `note` is null except while the changeset is landing, when it says that some members may already be on their trunks and the workspace is the proposed state, not the trunks. Members are the composable set: a member whose repository has been deleted is left out, and a changeset with no member left has `composition`, `tip` null and `members` empty

404.description: No such changeset, or a member the caller may not read

get.summary: How big this review is, member by member: the line counts behind `+412 − 77`, computed from the same tree diff /diff reports path by path. repo:read on every member; otherwise 404, masked identically to the changeset read.

200.description: { changeset, total: { files, insertions, deletions, truncated }, members: [{ repo, change, patchset, files, insertions, deletions, truncated }] } — members are in landing order, and each member's numbers are its latest patchset against its parent commit. `truncated` is true when at least one file was not counted: over 512 KiB (the same limit the diff view refuses to fetch as text), binary, a submodule pointer, or a rewrite past the request's work bound. The counts are then the total over the files that *were* counted, and `files` stays exact because it comes from the tree walk — a number invented for a file the server declined to read would be worse than an absent one. On the total, `truncated` means some member's is.

post.summary: Land every member, all or nothing. repo:write on every member.
post.description: Pre-flight first, and it writes nothing: every member must be `open`, its sufficiency verdict at the latest patchset green, its required checks **passing** — a check that has not reported is a refusal here where a single change would be held, because the plan below is made against the trunks as they stand now — and its patchset a fast-forward of its target. The changeset's composed CI is part of that gate too: a composed check failing, cancelled or skipped is a refusal, and one still queued or running is a `waiting` refusal here, the same as a member's own. Landing does not cancel composed runs. Then the commit point: one landing record with the full plan, and the changeset turns `landing` in the same transaction. From that row on the landing *will* finish, on this node or any other: members are CASed in landing order one manifest at a time; a member whose trunk moved in the window fails the landing, and every member already landed is put back with a **revert commit** on top of the landed one — never a rewind. `GET …/changesets/{changeset}` carries the landing's progress member by member until the changeset is `landed` or `failed`. A landed member is `landed` with `land_verdict` "landed with changeset {key}"; a reverted one is `open` again with a verdict naming the revert and what failed, and needs a new patchset to land again; a member that never got its turn is `open` with an `ejected:` verdict.

202.description: { queued: true, job, changeset, landing, plan: [{ repo, change, ref, old, new }] } — the plan in landing order: for each member the target ref, the tip it was judged against and will be CASed from, and the patchset commit it lands.

409.description: { error, gate, waiting_on } — `error` names the first member in landing order standing in the way (`repo/change: why`), or says `changeset is {state}` when it is not open. `gate` is what stands in the way, composed CI folded in — "waiting" when every member is approved and a required check has not reported, "blocked" for anything a person has to act on (a member not yet approved, a failing check, a trunk that moved) — and never "ready" in a refusal. `waiting_on` lists `repo/change: check` for every required check still to report; a `waiting` gate is a refusal here, so land again when it has reported. A member that is not a fast-forward of its trunk is `repo/change: not fast-forward from {tip}`, with `gate` "blocked".

post.summary: Revert a landed changeset: a new changeset, one call. repo:write on every member.
post.description: Body { key, title?, body? }. In every repository a member of this changeset landed in, makes one commit on a new `revert/{key}` branch off the target branch **as it is now** that puts back every path the member changed — the deleted file returns, the rewritten one is its old self at its old mode, the added ones are gone — and leaves every other path alone, so work landed since is kept. Each commit is registered as a change on the member's target exactly as a push would be (pinned, CI triggered, owners notified), and the changes are composed into changeset `key` with this changeset's edges **reversed**: what landed after its dependency is undone before it. Nothing about this changeset moves, and no trunk moves: the new changeset is reviewed under the same OWNERS and landed with `POST …/land` like any other. Only members recorded as landed are reverted — every member of a `landed` changeset, and of a `failed` one the members the unwind left landed (`GET …/changesets/{changeset}` shows them `done` with a `not reverted` note). Every member is checked before any branch is written, and any one refusal refuses the whole call: a path somebody has changed on trunk since the landing, a target branch that is gone, a `revert/{key}` branch already there, a member whose repository has been deleted. Title defaults to `Revert "{title}"`, body to `Reverts changeset {key}.`.

201.description: The new changeset, as `GET …/changesets/{key}` returns it, with `reverts` naming this one. Members are in the order the reverts were made; `order` is the landing order.

400.description: { error } — `key` is not a valid changeset key

404.description: No such changeset, or a member the caller may not write

409.description: { error, conflicts? } — `changeset is {state}: nothing of it has landed` for an open, landing or abandoned changeset; `changeset {key} already exists`; `nothing of changeset {key} is landed: every member that landed was reverted` for a failed changeset the unwind fully put back; `{repo}/{change}: the repository no longer exists`. When a member cannot be reverted cleanly, `error` names the first in landing order — `{repo}/{change}: {ref} has changed since it landed at {paths}`, `{repo}/{change}: {ref} no longer exists`, `{repo}/{change}: revert/{key} already exists` — and `conflicts` lists every such member as { repo, change, why, changed?: [path], no_branch?, branch_exists? }. Nothing was written.

Paging is keyset over `(namespace, name, id)` and the cursor is applied inside the visibility filter, so a tampered cursor moves the window and never widens it.

parameters.description: Narrow to repositories carrying exactly this topic. Case-insensitive, because topics are stored lowercased. A topic no repository carries — or a string that could not be a topic at all — returns an empty page rather than a 400, because a link somebody typed by hand should come back empty rather than as an error.

post.description: Enqueues a poll of the runs GitHub already has, through the org's existing App installation. Requires repo:write rather than org:admin — unlike an import this writes nothing anybody has to undo by hand, it restates verdicts a provider already reached, idempotently, into rows nobody edits. Refused before anything long-running starts, in a sentence naming the way through, for a repository whose origin is not a GitHub App installation: a poll that is accepted and then silently does nothing for a minute is a much worse answer. get.summary: The check verdicts standing beside one commit — one row per workflow, the newest of each
get.description: Not the commit's whole check history. Keyed on the workflow's name, because the name is what a reader recognises — the cost being that if two providers report a workflow of the same name for one commit, the newer wins and the other is not shown. Readable by anyone who may read the repository, a signed-out visitor included; a private repository answers exactly as one that does not exist. A commit with no runs, and a sha that could never have been stored, are both an empty list with 200: the 404 on this route belongs to the repository, and spending it on the commit too would make "no such project" and "nothing has built this yet" indistinguishable. The sha is deliberately not checked against a reachable object — a run can be reported for a commit since rewritten away, and refusing to show it would lose the only record that it happened.

get.summary: What the repository is, beside what is in it: the language mix by bytes, the detected licence, the community files (CONTRIBUTING / CODE_OF_CONDUCT / SECURITY) found at the root or in `.github/`, the path of the README, and the topics. Everything but the topics is derived from the tree at the default branch — no new git plumbing and nothing stored. Readable by anyone who may read the repository, a signed-out visitor included; masked exactly as the code is for anyone who may not. `license.spdx` is null with `recognised: false` when the file is there but the fingerprint table is not certain what it is — a wrong licence is materially worse than no licence, so it never guesses. get.description: What `.weft/` actually ran — as opposed to `/workflows`, which is what it *would* run. The sentence is in `error` and the machine-readable reason is in `blocked_reason` — `fork`, `budget` or `suspended`, and null unless the run is blocked. Branch on `blocked_reason`, never on the words in `error`: only a `fork` run can be started by `POST …/changes/{change}/workflows/approve`, and the sentences are written for a person and get rewritten. The run's mirrored check row is `queued` rather than failing, because nothing is wrong with the commit. Job JSON is `{ id, job_id, key, matrix, state, attempts, error, detail_url, log_chunks, started_at, completed_at }`; `key` is the expanded cell name and `matrix` is an object, already parsed. Every job also mirrors itself into `check_runs` as `<workflow> / <cell>`, so a run's verdicts appear on the Checks tab and in the land gate without asking here at all — except a `changeset` run, whose jobs mirror onto the changeset instead (`checks` on `GET …/changesets/{changeset}`) and never onto the commit. `limit` defaults to 20 and is clamped to 100 rather than refused: a limit is a hint about how much the renderer wants, and a 400 turns a harmless over-request into a broken page whose only recovery is guessing a maximum the caller cannot see.

The Checks tab asks for `changeset` to list the composed runs, which report to the changeset and never to a commit here and so appear nowhere among the check rows. An event word this server does not use answers an empty list rather than a 400.

get.description: `text/plain`. The complete log once the job has uploaded it, and the chunks produced so far while it is still running — the two are the same bytes read at different times, so no caller has to know which half of a job's life it is looking at. get.summary: A job's build log as it arrives (server-sent events)
get.description: `text/event-stream`. Emits `event: chunk` carrying `{ "text": ... }` for each new log chunk, in order, `event: queued` once for a job that has not started, and `event: done` carrying `{ "state": ... }` when the job leaves running/queued, after which the stream closes. The chunk is JSON rather than the raw bytes because an SSE `data:` field cannot carry a newline — the wire format splits a multi-line payload across several `data:` lines and loses the payload's trailing one, which would run the last line of each chunk into the first line of the next. Held open for at most six hours. The feed reads the same stored chunk objects the plain log route does rather than an in-memory fan-out from the runner: in a fleet, the node a runner posts to is not the node a reader is connected to, and an in-process channel would show the log to whoever happened to land on the right one and a spinner to everybody else.

get.summary: Everything a runner needs to check out and execute one job
get.description: For hosted runners; not a route a person calls. The credential is a **job token**: minted for one attempt of one job, `repo:read` on one repository, with an expiry, and recorded on the job row. A token that is valid for the repository but was not minted for this job is 403 — otherwise one build could report another's verdict. Refusals are ordered 401 (no or unknown token), 404 (no such job), 403 (wrong job), 410, so a job's state is only ever disclosed to the credential that owns it. One deliberate exception, and it is what makes cancellation work: a token that no longer authenticates — cancelling a job revokes its token before asking the platform to stop the container — is still answered **410 with the state** when it is the token this job was dispatched with and the job has stopped running. Anything else is 401. Without it the container being cancelled is refused at the door with a 401, which a runner retries, and it runs every remaining step before finding out. **410** `{ error, state }` means the job is no longer running — cancelled, superseded, already reported, or its repository deleted — and the runner's contract is to kill what it is doing and exit 0. That is the whole cancellation mechanism: there is no channel into the container, so "stop" is something a runner learns by being told on its next call. The answer is the job's frozen JobSpec (`image`, `timeout_minutes`, `env`, `steps`) plus `id`, `run_id`, `attempt`, `key`, `job`, `clone_url`, `fetch_ref`, `commit_sha`, `ref_name`, `event`, `change_key` and `matrix`. `clone_url` is built from the runner URL the runner already reached this API on rather than the public host — they are the same behind a CDN and differ on a private network — and never carries a credential — the token goes in a header the runner sets itself, so it cannot end up in a remote's config, a reflog, or a `ps` listing. `fetch_ref` is `refs/heads/<branch>` for a push and `refs/patchsets/<sha>` for a change, because a change's commits are not on a branch. When `event` is `changeset` the answer also carries `changeset`: `{ key, members: [{ repo, change, clone_url, fetch_ref, commit_sha, token }] }` in member order, every member of the changeset at the head it proposes, which the runner checks out side by side under a workspace directory and runs the steps in this job's own repository. The job's own member has `token: null` — it is checked out with the job token — and every other member carries a **plaintext `repo:read` token minted for that one repository**, expiring with the job token and revoked with it when the job finishes or is stopped; a re-fetch of the spec mints a fresh set and revokes the previous one. It is deliberately not one org-wide token: a member's CI script is code its author wrote, and an org-wide read would let it read repositories the author cannot see. The top-level `fetch_ref`, `commit_sha` and `change_key` stay this job's own member's.

401.description: no, unknown, revoked or expired job token

403.description: that token was not minted for this job

404.description: no such job

410.description: { error, state } — the job is no longer running; stop and exit

A `seq` at or below what has already been recorded is a retry: the object is overwritten and the answer is still 200, because the counter only moves forward and a re-sent chunk must not hide chunks a reader has already been shown. Answering also renews the job's lease: a job producing output is a job that is alive, so a build that logs steadily never needs a separate heartbeat. The credential is a **job token**: minted for one attempt of one job, `repo:read` on one repository, with an expiry, and recorded on the job row. A token that is valid for the repository but was not minted for this job is 403 — otherwise one build could report another's verdict. Refusals are ordered 401 (no or unknown token), 404 (no such job), 403 (wrong job), 410, so a job's state is only ever disclosed to the credential that owns it. One deliberate exception, and it is what makes cancellation work: a token that no longer authenticates — cancelling a job revokes its token before asking the platform to stop the container — is still answered **410 with the state** when it is the token this job was dispatched with and the job has stopped running. Anything else is 401. Without it the container being cancelled is refused at the door with a 401, which a runner retries, and it runs every remaining step before finding out. **410** `{ error, state }` means the job is no longer running — cancelled, superseded, already reported, or its repository deleted — and the runner's contract is to kill what it is doing and exit 0. That is the whole cancellation mechanism: there is no channel into the container, so "stop" is something a runner learns by being told on its next call.

400.description: malformed body, or a seq below 1

401.description: no, unknown, revoked or expired job token

403.description: that token was not minted for this job

404.description: no such job

post.summary: The same upload, for a `.pypirc` whose `repository` carries a trailing slash. Registered rather than redirected, because a client does not re-POST a body after a redirect.

get.summary: pip's Simple API and the files it links to. `simple/` is the root index, `simple/{name}/` is one project's page — PEP 503, with a `#sha256=` fragment on every link, which is what pip verifies a download against — and `files/{name}/{filename}` is one artifact. Asking for `simple/{name}` without the trailing slash answers 301: pip resolves a link relative to the page it read, so without the slash every filename would resolve one directory up. Requires package:read. A project nobody has published is an **empty page**, not a 404, because pip has read a 404 from an index as the index being broken.

200.description: the index page as text/html, or the artifact as application/octet-stream

301.description: a project page asked for without its trailing slash

401.description: no credential, with a Basic challenge

404.description: no such org, PyPI is not enabled for it, or no such file

put.summary: `cargo publish`. The body is framed rather than JSON: a little-endian u32 length, the metadata document, a second length, and the `.crate` bytes. Every length is checked against what is actually left before it is used. Requires package:write. Cargo sends its credential as a **bare** `Authorization` value with no scheme, which this registry reads; `license` in the metadata is already an SPDX expression by Cargo's own rule, so it is stored as it stands. A published version is immutable.

200.description: { warnings: { invalid_categories, invalid_badges, other } } — Cargo prints whatever is in here, so an empty set is the quiet success

400.description: a malformed frame, metadata that is not what cargo sends, or a crate name that cannot be stored

401.description: no credential, with a Basic challenge

409.description: that version is already uploaded, or the name is a proxied package

get.summary: `{verb}` is `download`: the `.crate` bytes, at the URL Cargo builds by appending `/{crate}/{version}/download` to the `dl` in config.json. Requires package:read. A yanked version still downloads — a yank means “do not resolve to this unless a lockfile already names it”, and removing the bytes would break every build that pinned it.

200.description: the .crate file

401.description: no credential, with a Basic challenge

404.description: no such org, Cargo is not enabled for it, no such crate or version, or a verb other than download

delete.summary: `cargo yank`. `{verb}` is `yank`. Requires package:write. The index is assembled from rows on every read, so this is visible to the next resolve rather than after something rewrites a file.

200.description: { ok: true }

401.description: no credential, with a Basic challenge

404.description: no such crate or version

put.summary: `cargo yank --undo`. `{verb}` is `unyank`. Requires package:write.

200.description: { ok: true }

401.description: no credential, with a Basic challenge

404.description: no such crate or version

get.summary: Cargo's sparse index. `index/config.json` names the download and API bases and sets `auth-required`, without which Cargo never sends a credential and every request arrives anonymous. `index/{prefix}/{name}` is one crate as newline-delimited JSON, one object per version, in publication order — and the prefix must be the one Cargo's own length rule produces (`1/a`, `2/ab`, `3/a/abc`, `ab/cd/abcd`), so one crate has exactly one URL. Requires package:read.

200.description: config.json, or the crate's index file as text/plain

401.description: no credential, with a Basic challenge

404.description: no such org, Cargo is not enabled for it, no such crate, or a prefix that is not the one Cargo would ask for

get.summary: The npm registry. `{path}` is the package — a scoped name arrives as two segments or percent-encoded, and both reach the same package — or, when it contains npm's `/-/` marker, the tarball the packument named. Requires package:read, which org:read carries. A 401 here carries a `WWW-Authenticate: Basic` challenge, unlike the rest of this API, because a registry client has no other way to learn it should send the token from its `.npmrc`. An organization that has not switched npm on answers 404 for everything, indistinguishably from one that does not exist.

200.description: the packument — `{ name, _id, versions, dist-tags }`, where each version is the manifest as published with a `dist` block naming a tarball URL, its sha1 `shasum` and its `sha512-` `integrity`, both computed from the stored bytes — or, for a tarball path, the artifact as `application/octet-stream`.

401.description: no credential, with a Basic challenge

404.description: no such org, npm is not enabled for it, or no such package or tarball

put.summary: Publish one version, in npm's publish-document shape: the version manifest under `versions` and the tarball base64 in `_attachments`. Requires package:write, which repo:write deliberately does **not** carry. A published version is immutable — republishing one answers 409 and changes nothing — and the attachment's declared `length` and `dist.shasum` are checked against the decoded bytes before anything is stored.

201.description: { ok, id, rev }

400.description: the document is malformed, names a different package than the URL, carries more than one version or attachment, or the attachment disagrees with its own declared length or shasum

401.description: no credential, with a Basic challenge

404.description: no such org, or npm is not enabled for it

409.description: that version is already published, or the name is one this org caches from an upstream registry

413.description: the artifact is over the size limit

get.summary: Which package ecosystems this organization admits. Requires org:read. Always returns a row for every ecosystem the deployment knows, including the ones nobody has configured — those read `off`, which is the default and means the registry answers for nothing.

200.description: { ecosystems: [{ ecosystem, label, mode, license_unknown }], registry_base } — `mode` is one of `off`, `private`, `proxy`; `license_unknown` says what to do with a package whose licence cannot be determined, and is per ecosystem because most container images declare none. `registry_base` is the URL a client configures against.

401.description: no credential

404.description: no such org, or it is not visible to this caller

put.summary: Switch one ecosystem on or off. Requires org:admin, and deliberately not package:write: this changes what an organization's builds may reach. Omitting `license_unknown` leaves the existing disposition alone, so enabling an ecosystem does not quietly reset a policy somebody set.

200.description: { ecosystem, label, mode, license_unknown }

400.description: unknown ecosystem, mode, or disposition

401.description: no credential

404.description: no such org, or the caller is not an admin of it

get.summary: The admission policy: what may enter this organization's builds from an upstream registry, and what happens when something may not. Requires org:read — a developer whose install was refused has to be able to read why without an admin in the room. The optional `ecosystem` query parameter selects which reserved-namespace list is returned and defaults to `npm`.

200.description: { ecosystem, mode, cooldown_days, license_mode, license_rules: [{ spdx_id, disposition }], reserved: [pattern] } — `mode` is `audit` (record what would have been refused and serve anyway) or `block`; `cooldown_days` holds an upstream release younger than that many days, with 0 disabling it; `license_mode` is `allow_list` (only what is listed enters) or `deny_list` (everything except).

401.description: no credential

404.description: no such org, or it is not visible to this caller

put.summary: Set the mode, the cooldown and the licence mode. Requires org:admin. New organizations start at `audit` with no cooldown and a deny list, which admits everything and records nothing: a policy that blocks from day one meets a deadline in week one and gets switched off.

200.description: the policy, as GET returns it

400.description: unknown mode or licence mode, or a cooldown outside 0..=3650 days

401.description: no credential

404.description: no such org, or the caller is not an admin of it

put.summary: Add, change or remove one licence rule. Requires org:admin. Body is { spdx_id, disposition } where `disposition` is `allow`, `deny`, or absent to remove the rule. Removing is not the same as denying: under a deny list an absent rule admits, and under an allow list it refuses. Identifiers are compared case-insensitively, as SPDX defines them.

200.description: the policy, as GET /packages/policy returns it

400.description: an empty identifier, or a disposition other than allow or deny

401.description: no credential

404.description: no such org, or the caller is not an admin of it

post.summary: Claim a name prefix that is never fetched from an upstream registry. Requires org:admin. Body is { ecosystem, pattern }. This closes the hole the “private always wins” rule leaves: that rule protects a name already published here, so without a reservation somebody who registers `@acme/new-service` upstream first answers for it. Matched on a segment boundary, so `@acme` covers `@acme/widget` and not `@acmecorp/widget`.

200.description: the policy, as GET /packages/policy returns it

400.description: unknown ecosystem, or an empty or over-long prefix

401.description: no credential

404.description: no such org, or the caller is not an admin of it

delete.summary: Release a reserved prefix, named by the `ecosystem` and `pattern` query parameters. Requires org:admin — this is the widening direction, since the name becomes proxyable again.

400.description: unknown ecosystem

401.description: no credential

404.description: no such org, the caller is not an admin of it, or that prefix was never reserved

get.summary: What the admission policy has caught, most recent first. Requires org:read. Deduplicated to one row per (ecosystem, name, version) with a hit count, so a CI run resolving eight hundred dependencies does not write eight hundred rows. `limit` is an optional query parameter, clamped to 500.

200.description: { findings: [{ ecosystem, name, version, disposition, rule, reason, hits, first_at, last_at }] } — `disposition` is `blocked` when the package was refused and `would_block` when audit mode served it anyway; `rule` is `reserved`, `cooldown` or `license`; `reason` is the sentence the client printed.

401.description: no credential

404.description: no such org, or it is not visible to this caller

delete.summary: Forget one finding, named by the `ecosystem`, `name` and `version` query parameters. Requires org:admin. This does not admit the package — the rule that produced the row is still in force and the next fetch writes it again. Allowing something is a change to the rule, and clearing the row afterwards is what makes a cleared row mean somebody acted rather than somebody tidied.

400.description: unknown ecosystem

401.description: no credential

404.description: no such org, the caller is not an admin of it, or there is no such finding

get.summary: What this organization holds, newest activity first. Requires package:read. `ecosystem`, `limit` and `offset` are optional query parameters.

200.description: { packages: [{ id, ecosystem, name, private, origin, created_at, updated_at }] } — `origin` is `local` for a package published here and `proxied` for one cached from an upstream registry.

400.description: unknown ecosystem

401.description: no credential

404.description: no such org, or it is not visible to this caller

get.summary: One package, its versions and its tags. Requires package:read. Each version carries the repository, commit and job that produced it, which is the question asked during an incident and the reason this registry sits beside the code.

200.description: the package, plus `versions: [{ id, version, yanked, yank_reason, license, license_source, size_bytes, repo_id, commit_sha, job_id, published_by, published_at }]` and `tags: [{ tag, version }]`. `license_source` is `declared`, `detected` or `unknown`.

401.description: no credential

404.description: no such org or package, or it is not visible to this caller

delete.summary: Take the whole package down. Requires org:admin, not package:write — unpublishing something everybody depends on is the one irreversible act here, and a CI token that may publish should not also be able to do it. The bytes stay until the collector has proved nothing else references them.

401.description: no credential

404.description: no such org or package, or the caller is not an admin of it

post.summary: Hide a version from resolution, or put it back — `{ yanked, reason }`. Requires package:write. Not a delete, and there is no delete: a yanked version still downloads by exact version, so a lockfile that already names it keeps building. Removing it outright would break every pipeline that pinned it.

200.description: the version, as `GET …/packages/{package}` returns it

400.description: that is not a version string this registry could have stored

401.description: no credential

404.description: no such org, package or version, or it is not visible to this caller
